title: [no-ci] [precompile] Add save() checkpoints and summary() to Dynamo captures
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #198217
* __->__ #198227
* #198138
* #198216
* #198137
* #198215
* #198136
* #198214
* #198243
* #198135
* #198213
* #197993
* #198284
* #198283
* #198223
* #198211

**Problem.** A Dynamo capture wrote its artifact only when the `with` block exited cleanly, so a job that died mid-loop left nothing on disk, and there was no way to read the coverage or guard report the session had built up.

**Fix.** `_DynamoCapture` gains `save()`, which checkpoints everything captured so far to the same two files without ending the capture, and `summary()`, which returns the session's `PrecompileSummary` inside the block and after it.

**Summary.** A Dynamo capture that dies mid-loop left nothing on disk, because the artifact was rendered and written only on a clean exit. `_DynamoCapture.save()` now renders and writes everything captured so far to the same `artifact_path` / `cache_path` pair without ending the capture, so each call re-renders and rewrites both files and a job that dies between saves leaves the last checkpoint loadable, while a gate refusal or a write failure raises and writes nothing partial with the capture still open. Exit writes only when there are calls the last save did not cover, tracked as the call count the last write saw, which starts at `-1` so a block that never called still raises the nothing-captured error rather than writing an empty artifact. Calls and saves share the capture's one lock, so a `save()` never snapshots the capture mid-compile, and a `save()` from inside `fn` is refused. `summary()` exposes the session's `PrecompileSummary` -- coverage, recompilation, failure and guard information for everything captured so far -- readable inside the block and after it, including after a gate refusal, since the refusal is raised only after teardown.

## Where this fits

The stack replaces the callable `torch.compiler.precompile(fn, *example_inputs)` (trace once on inputs passed up front, pair returned in memory) with a caller-driven context manager: `capture(fn, artifact_path=, cache_path=)` is entered with a `with` block, the caller calls it on as many example inputs as they like (each graph break and recompiled variant is folded in), the `(python_code, cache)` pair is written to the two files on exit, and `load(artifact_path, cache_path)` serves it in a fresh process. The end-to-end example and the PR-by-PR map live in #197993's "The new API, end to end" section. This PR adds `cap.save()` checkpoints and `cap.summary()` (coverage, recompiles, dropped guards) to the multi-call `DynamoTracer` capture from #198138.

## save() checkpoints mid-block

The parent wrote once, from `__exit__`. `save()` is the same `_write()` -- `snapshot_artifact(**self._gates)` then `_write_artifact` -- callable from inside the block, behind the same three refusals a call has (not entered or already exited, inside `fn`, nothing captured yet):

```python
with capture(step, artifact_path=artifact, cache_path=cache, tracer=DynamoTracer()) as cap:
    cap.save()                 # PrecompileError: nothing was captured ...
    cap(model, x2)
    cap.save()                 # renders + rewrites m.py and m.cache with the first call
    cap(model, x3)             # recompiled variant; not on disk yet
# exit: the block has a call the last save did not cover -> both files rewritten
```

Each `save()` rewrites both files from scratch, so the checkpoint after `x2` and the final artifact after `x3` differ. A `require_*` gate refusal or an `OSError` from the rewrite raises out of `save()` as a `PrecompileError`; `_write_artifact` leaves the previous pair in place, so the last good checkpoint is still loadable and the capture stays open for more calls or another `save()`.

`test_save_checkpoints_mid_block` pins this: the pre-call `save()` raises `"nothing was captured"`, the checkpoint after the first call is read back, and the artifact after exit is not byte-equal to it.

## Exit writes only what the last save did not cover

Exit tracks the call count the last write saw:

```python
# __init__
self._saved_calls = -1          # not 0: a block that never called is still dirty at exit

# _write, after _write_artifact succeeds
self._saved_calls = self._calls

# __exit__: parent wrote on every clean exit
if exc[0] is None:
# now
if exc[0] is None and self._calls > self._saved_calls:
```

So a block whose last `save()` covered every call writes nothing at exit, a block with calls after the last `save()` writes a final checkpoint, and a block that never called (`_calls` is 0, above the `-1` start) still reaches the `"nothing was captured"` error instead of writing an empty artifact. A block that raised still writes nothing, as before.

## summary() inside and after the block

```python
with capture(step, artifact_path=artifact, cache_path=cache, tracer=DynamoTracer()) as cap:
    cap(model, x2)
    cap(model, x3, scale=0.5)
    summary = cap.summary()
summary.complete           # True
summary.frames             # 2: the entry and its graph-break continuation
summary.resume_functions   # 1
summary.guarded_codes      # >= 3: a variant per call the guards told apart
```

`summary()` is `self._map(self._session.summary)`, so `PackageError` / `RecompileError` surface as `PrecompileError` like every other session call. It is readable after a gate refusal too, because `__exit__` holds the refusal and re-raises it only after teardown:

```python
with self.assertRaisesRegex(PrecompileError, "captured call raised"):
    with capture(step, ...) as cap:
        cap(model, x2)
        with self.assertRaises(RuntimeError):
            cap(model, torch.randn(2, 5))
        cap.summary().complete     # False: the raised call is a coverage gap
# nothing written: neither m.py nor m.cache exists
```

The dropped guards move from being documented as an artifact list (`DROPPED_GUARDS`) to being reported through `Capture.summary`; the artifact still lists the same slots:

```python
with capture(single, ...) as cap:
    cap(model, x2)
    summary = cap.summary()
"MODULE_MATCH" in summary.dropped_guard_types   # the default filter drops the model identity guard
summary.kept_guards                             # non-empty
summary.risky_dropped_guards                    # ()
for guard_type, source in summary.dropped_guards:
    assert f"[{guard_type!r}, {source!r}]" in open(artifact).read()
```

`test_dropped_guards_are_reported_in_the_summary_and_the_artifact` reads the default filter's drops from the summary and checks the artifact lists the same `(guard_type, source)` slots; `test_the_strict_gate_refuses_dropped_guards` keeps the `DynamoTracer(require_no_dropped_guards=True)` refusal on its own. `test_graph_breaks_and_recompiles_round_trip_in_a_fresh_process` and `test_a_raised_call_is_refused_at_exit_and_writes_nothing` gain the summary assertions shown above.

Test Plan:

`test_save_checkpoints_mid_block` checkpoints after the first call and checks the exit rewrite after the second; `test_dropped_guards_are_reported_in_the_summary_and_the_artifact` reads the default filter's drops from the summary and the artifact; the round-trip and raised-call tests gain their summary assertions.

```
python test/test_precompile.py
lintrunner -a torch/_precompile.py test/test_precompile.py
```

title: Keep RNG ops working, and rank-agnostic, under compile_on_one_rank
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #196154
* #196153
* __->__ #196152
* #196940
* #196939
* #196938
* #196150
* #196151
* #197585

Every RNG op failed to compile under compile_on_one_rank -- rand, randn, randint
and so dropout too:

  RuntimeError: prims::inductor_seed() Expected a value of type 'Device'
                for argument 'device' but instead found type 'Node'

replace_random and replace_randint run on the joint graph, where a factory op's
device operand is still a coor current_device() node: respecialize_current_device_nodes
does not concretise those until post_grad. Both handlers take that operand
straight off the matched node, so a graph node reached inductor_prims.seed(),
whose schema declares Device and cannot accept one.

Resolve the node where a real device is genuinely needed, and only there:

  - get_device(), which feeds inductor_prims.seed()
  - fuse_seed_creation_pass, when it builds meta["val"] for the fused seed --
    the graph argument beside it keeps the node, which is what makes the fused
    seed rank-agnostic

Anything else that turns out to be a graph node now raises rather than being
silently mishandled.

That alone leaves the seed's device baked, because fwd_only -- the tracer behind
every replace_by_example -- disables compile_on_one_rank wholesale. That is right
for a pattern template, which is only ever matched against, and wrong for a
replacement, which is spliced into the user's graph and so bakes a rank-specific
device into it. Split the two: fwd_only keeps the feature live when tracing a
replacement, and the fourteen template call sites are unaffected.

The RNG path is now device-agnostic in the joint graph:

  inductor_seeds_default = prims.inductor_seeds.default(1, current_device_default_1)

where it previously read device(type='cuda', index=0).

title: Drop the device index from the fx graph cache key under compile_on_one_rank
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #196154
* __->__ #196153
* #196152
* #196940
* #196939
* #196938
* #196150
* #196151
* #197585

Every rank compiled the same graph and then missed on every other rank's cache
entry, so no compiled artifact was ever shared. The index reaches the key through
exactly one component -- example_inputs' TensorMetadata:

  [lfqb4cez...] example_inputs[0]: TensorMetadata(..., device=device(type='cuda', index=0), ...)

Nothing else contributes one. In particular the graph hashed alongside it does
not: the key is built in _compile_fx_inner before _recursive_post_grad_passes
runs, so it sees the AOT graph, where devices are still current_device() nodes.
Measured on a 16-GPU CooR job, 4730 device-bearing key lines per rank, all of
them example_inputs, and zero from gm.

Strip it in extract_tensor_metadata_for_cache_key, whose stated job is removing
fields not needed for caching, and which already does this for storage_offset
and storage_bytes. Gated on the accelerator being the current one, so cpu
tensors and non-CooR compiles keep their index -- outside CooR several devices
can legitimately be live and must not collide.

The full key is now byte-identical across devices under CooR, and still
correctly distinct without it.

test_inductor_compiled_on_one_device_runs_on_another asserted a cache *miss* as
a deliberate tripwire for this change -- its comment asked that landing a
device-agnostic key trip the test rather than silently widen it. It now asserts
the hit. That comment also flagged CompiledFxGraph.device_idxs as a second
requirement for reuse; the reused artifact was checked to run on the reusing
rank's own device and to be numerically correct, so no change is needed there.

body:

* #196152
* #196940
* __->__ #196939
* #196938
* #196150
* #196151
* #197585

After tensor devices became runtime-relative under compile_on_one_rank, Dynamo
could no longer pass x.device through the stream constructor's constant-only
example path. Converting it to the tracing rank's device without retaining its
origin would instead reconstruct the stream on the wrong rank.

Build the example stream from the device's index-less form, which resolves to
the tracing rank's current device, while keeping the runtime-relative device
for reconstruction. This preserves both positional and keyword construction for
generic and CUDA streams.

An explicit device index -- Stream(0), Stream("cuda:0"), device_index=0 --
names the compiling rank's GPU and would be reconstructed as that GPU on every
rank. Under compile_on_one_rank it is now refused with
CompileOnOneRankUnsupported, matching how explicit-index device contexts are
refused.

torch.Event(device=x.device) goes through the same constant-only path and is
not fixed here.

title: Make tensor device observations rank-portable under compile_on_one_rank
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.17.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #196154
* #196153
* #196152
* #196940
* #196939
* #196938
* #196150
* __->__ #196151
* #197585

Dynamo specializes tensor device metadata before make_fx runs. Under
compile_on_one_rank, baking the current accelerator index into a guard, an FX
constant, or Tensor.get_device() makes the artifact rank-specific: another rank
can either recompile unnecessarily or silently observe the tracing rank's index.

Classify an indexed accelerator as runtime-relative only when it is the current
accelerator under CooR. x.device uses a dedicated variable that keeps the
accelerator type static and resolves index-dependent observations at runtime.
Tensor guards still check the exact index at this commit; #196150 relaxes them
to check against the runtime current device using the same classification.
Tensor.get_device() uses the same coor::current_device_index SymInt operator as
x.device, whose fake implementation leaves the index unbacked until execution.

An exact index guard would preserve eager specialization but defeat CooR by
creating one artifact per rank. Returning only an index-less device works for
factory and .to() passthrough but loses observable index semantics. The runtime
index representation preserves both: device passthrough remains portable, while
arithmetic reads the executing rank's index and data-dependent control flow
graph-breaks rather than specializing to the tracing rank.

The index observation is cached per tracer, not per graph. A higher-order op
traces each subgraph with its own tracer, and a proxy created under a sibling
cannot be lifted into this one -- both branches of a torch.cond reading
x.device.index otherwise trip the root-tracer assertion in
lift_tracked_freevar_to_input.

torch.device(d) copies d: the result is equal to it but a distinct object, so
the call hands back a fresh rank-relative device rather than d itself, and the
device= keyword form is accepted as well. Handing back a distinct variable is
what keeps `torch.device(d) is d` False the way it is eagerly, so identity
comparison is taught that two of these are never the same object -- the same
rule a bound method already follows, and the same reason `x.device is x.device`
is False.

Equality reports one equal to an explicit cuda:N whenever N is the running
rank's index, so its hash has to agree with every cuda:N. Under CooR both it and
a constant torch.device hash as the index-less device, so all devices of one
type share a bucket and equality decides: two rank-relative devices are the same
key (which is what _group_tensors_by_device_and_dtype, and so
clip_grad_norm_, needs), and against an explicit cuda:N the key comparison reads
the runtime index -- a data-dependent error under fullgraph, a graph break
otherwise, the same as `x.device == torch.device("cuda:N")`. Refusing to hash
was the alternative, but it made clip_grad_norm_ fail to compile under CooR.

CompileOnOneRankUnsupported, for a construct CooR cannot express at all, is
raised by later commits in the stack; it propagates whether or not graph breaks
are allowed, which is why it is its own type rather than an Unsupported or a
UserError -- convert_frame soft-fails both of those.

The tensorless index operator is assigned a CPU lowering device because
FallbackKernel otherwise has no tensor from which to infer one.

Test Plan:

```shell
TORCHINDUCTOR_COMPILE_THREADS=1 .venv/bin/python test/distributed/tensor/test_compile_on_one_rank.py TestCompileOnOneRankDeviceAsParameter TestCompileOnOneRankLegacyCollective

```

title: [MPS] Fix silent corruption in bmm for non-contiguous inputs > 2**32 elements
body:
Fixes #197636.

### Description
This PR addresses a critical bug in the MPS backend where `bmm` silently returns corrupted outputs (and corrupted gradients on the backward pass) when the output exceeds 2**32 elements and the inputs are non-contiguous views (e.g., in eager attention `q @ k.transpose()`). 

**Root Cause:**
When inputs cross the 2**32 element threshold, `bmm_out_mps_impl` routes them to `tiled_bmm_out_mps_impl`. However, `tiled_bmm_out_mps_impl` passes the raw `MTLBuffer` objects directly to `MPSNDArrayDescriptor` without accounting for memory strides. For transposed or sliced inputs, the Metal kernel blindly reads the memory sequentially, causing complete math corruption. 

Because the backward pass calculates gradients using `bmm(G, b.transpose(-1, -2))`, this lack of a `.contiguous()` check also silently corrupts the backward gradients even when the forward pass inputs were perfectly contiguous.

**Fix:**
We explicitly enforce `.contiguous()` on both `batch1` and `batch2` immediately before routing to the `tiled_bmm_out_mps_impl` function. This forces PyTorch to pack the memory into a row-major layout, allowing the Metal tiled kernel to read the correct values safely and resolving both the forward and backward pass corruptions.

### Testing
- Relying on PyTorch CI for MPS regression test suites.
- Resolves the exact reproduction harness outlined in Issue #197636.

title: [benchmarks/dynamo] Use small-output accuracy policy for SigLIP
body:
## Summary
The next Triton pin bump will include https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/pull/11189, which updates Triton’s bundled CUDA libdevice. This change is not included in PyTorch's current Triton pin. 

In particular, the Triton PR changes the implementation used for float32 `erf` (`__nv_erff`). On A10G, we observed that the updated `__nv_erff` changes GELU rounding in `vit_base_patch16_siglip_256`. This causes the benchmark’s synthetic training loss to fail its accuracy check:
  - Failing test: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/35206051520/job/105174646954
  - Eager RMSE against FP64: 0.13545
  - Compiled RMSE against FP64: 0.47106
  - Ratio: 3.48×
  - Current limit: 3×

We isolated the failure to the updated `__nv_erff`; when we restored only its previous implementation, the accuracy failure disappeared. We also verified that the updated implementation remains within 1 ULP of correctly rounded FP64 (while CUDA permits up to 2 ULP) so this is expected numerical variation from the new implementation.

The failure is limited to the synthetic scalar loss that the benchmark creates to run backward. Inference and all other training results still pass with the existing thresholds.

This PR adds SigLIP to the existing small-output policy similar to what has been previously done (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/177042 for example) to allow a larger multiplier for small tensors.

## Test plan
  - Both affected A10G TIMM shards pass with this change:
    https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/35167626498
  - `erff` accuracy sweep:
    https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/34736991855
  - Nonscalar training results pass:
    https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/34738810460

title: [Lint] Add TEST_LINTER linter for testcase linter checks
body:
## Summary

Add a new `TEST_LINTER` linter that ensures every `TestCase` subclass satisfy the test case requirements.

This linter enforces test case requirements, including hardware classification declaration, test instantiation patterns, test method signatures, and supported decorators.



## Rules

All test classes inheriting from `TestCase` must first declare a valid `hw_classification` attribute. Supported values are `GENERIC`, `ACCELERATOR`,`CPU`, `CUDA`, `MPS`, and `XPU`.

The requirements for each `hw_classification` are summarized below:

GENERIC:

   - Class must not be used with instantiate_device_type_tests.
   - Test methods must not accept device/devices parameter.

ACCELERATOR:

   - Class must be used with instantiate_device_type_tests.
   - Every test method must accept device/devices parameter.
   - Test methods must not use `@only*` decorators (except @onlyAccelerator).
   - instantiate_device_type_tests must not use only_for (use except_for as a blacklist approach instead).

CPU / CUDA / MPS / XPU (device-specific):

   - Class must be used with instantiate_device_type_tests.
   - Every test method must accept device/devices parameter.
   - instantiate_device_type_tests must use only_for matching the device (e.g. only_for='cuda').
   - instantiate_device_type_tests must not use except_for.



## Changes

- `.lintrunner.toml`: register `TEST_LINTER` linter for `test/**/test_*.py` and `test/**/*_test.py`, excluding openreg and cpython tests.
- `tools/linter/adapters/test_linter.py`: the linter script.
- `tools/linter/adapters/test_linter_allowlist.json`: allowlist of files not yet classified (1191 entries covering all current test files).
- `tools/test/test_test_linter.py`: unit tests covering missing/invalid/`GENERIC`/`ACCELERATOR`/`CUDA`/non-test scenarios.

title: [c10d] Allow CPU device_id in init_process_group
body:
_new_process_group_helper rejected any CPU device_id, even one with a valid index (e.g. cpu:0), raising ValueError: init_process_group device_id parameter must be an accelerator with an index. This made it impossible to use device_id with the GLOO backend on CPU, despite init_process_group itself already treating CPU device_id as a valid case (it skips the accelerator-matching checks specifically for CPU, at line ~2513).

The restriction traces back to when device_id was CUDA-only, added to support NCCL's early-connect optimization (ncclCommSplit). A later commit (#143735) generalized the check to also allow XPU, but the CPU exclusion was carried forward unchanged rather than reconsidered.

This relaxes the check to only require a valid index, regardless of device type, and updates the error message and docstring to match. Tested manually with a two-rank torch.multiprocessing.spawn GLOO group confirming dist.barrier() succeeds across both ranks with device_id=torch.device("cpu:0"), not just single-rank initialization. Added test_device_id_cpu (confirms the fix) and test_device_id_cpu_no_index (confirms a missing index still correctly raises) to test_c10d_gloo.py.

Note: could not verify backend/device-type mismatch handling (e.g. nccl + cpu) since NCCL isn't compiled on this machine (Apple Silicon has no CUDA); confirmed the attempt still fails, but at a different point (RuntimeError: Distributed package doesn't have NCCL built in), before any real semantic check would run. Would appreciate a maintainer with GPU access double-checking that specific combination.

Also ran the full test_c10d_gloo.py suite: 48 pre-existing failures in ProcessGroupGlooLazyInitTest, unrelated to this change — confirmed via git stash that they fail identically without this fix applied.

Fixes #160731

title: Anchor torch's installed artifacts on the import system, not on `__file__`
body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #195293, which #195295 closed by fixing the reported symptom. This fixes the path-resolution mechanism underneath it, including a hard `import torch` failure that nothing had reported and a defect that made #195295 itself correct only some of the time, and then applies the mechanism to three call sites that were waiting on it. Fixes #191752.

Redirect-mode editable installs (scikit-build-core) are the first layout where Python sources and CMake-installed artifacts live in different trees: `.py` in the checkout, `include/ lib/ bin/ share/` beside the installed distribution. Two lookups added in #180247 to cope with that ask a question a source checkout can answer wrongly.

**`_load_global_deps`** fell back to `importlib.metadata.distribution("torch")`, which returns the *first* torch distribution on `sys.path`, not necessarily the installed one. A checkout carrying a setuptools-era `torch.egg-info` supplies a nearer match whose `locate_file` resolves into the checkout, the `exists()` guard declines it, and `CDLL` proceeds with the path it already knew was missing. `import torch` fails, and since the `OSError` is routed through the CUDA-dependency retry it surfaces as an unrelated dlopen error naming the source tree.

**`_compute_torch_parent`** only consulted the distribution when `bin/` was absent beside the module. `tools/build_libtorch.py` installs into `<repo>/torch` by design (`docs/libtorch.rst` documents that flow), so a checkout can hold one while the artifacts that matter live elsewhere. The presence test then kept the fallback from firing and `get_file_path("torch")` silently returned the source tree, which made every caller conditionally wrong, including the already-merged #195295.

Both now ask the import system where torch is installed, through one helper, `_installed_torch_dir`, in the order RFC-0060 (pytorch/rfcs#109) prescribes:

1. the editable loader's `paths` (scikit-build/scikit-build-core#1567, in review): the entry that is not the checkout and holds `lib/`. Identity, not `lib/`, is what excludes the checkout, since `torch/lib` is a tracked source directory; the order of `paths` is only fixed by scikit-build/scikit-build-core#1566, hence the probe rather than `paths[0]`;
2. `importlib.util.find_spec("torch._C").origin`, the directory `_C` will actually be imported from in every layout, and the anchor `torch/__init__.py` already uses for the Windows DLL directory. This is the path every released scikit-build-core hits today;
3. `__file__`, only when there is no spec at all (`BUILD_LIBTORCH_WHL`, a frozen interpreter).

Instead of reasoning around leftovers, the helper detects them: in a checkout whose `_C` resolves elsewhere, an in-tree `_C`, `lib/*.so`, `bin/`, `include/`, `share/` or `torch.egg-info` produces a warning listing the paths and pointing at `spin clean`. A warning rather than an error, because the editable finder maps `_C` and every other CMake-installed module by name to the install tree, so the stale copies are never imported; they only mislead tooling that walks metadata or `__file__`.

`_load_global_deps` resolves through `get_file_path` like every other consumer and raises `OSError` when the library is missing, which is what `ctypes.CDLL` raised and what `torch.utils.collect_env` catches.

With `get_file_path` sound, three further commits apply it to call sites that derived an asset path from `__file__`. **`torch.utils.cmake_prefix_path`** computed `share/cmake` with no fallback at all, so `find_package(Torch)` failed against every editable install; it is a public API, documented in `docs/cpp/source/installing.md`, and gets a regression test that asserts `Torch/TorchConfig.cmake` is actually present. **`torch/_inductor/codegen/mps.py`** embedded `c10/metal/*.h` from `Path(__file__).parent.parent.parent / "include"` on the cpp_wrapper path, the twin of the site #195295 fixed. **`torch_openreg`'s `get_pytorch_dir()`** passed `dirname(torch.__file__)` as `-DPYTORCH_INSTALL_DIR`. The last two are taken from #192559 by @guptaishaan.

**Revision history.** The first revision of this PR resolved the installed tree through `importlib.metadata.distributions()` with a METADATA-versus-PKG-INFO filter, and was reviewed in that form on 2026-09-04. A self-review found the indirection leaking (a built checkout shadowing a wheel could pair the wheel's `libtorch_global_deps` with the checkout's `_C`), and the review's `bin/`-probe finding pointed the same way; the import-system anchor replaces it. The reply below the review maps each of its points to the current revision.

**Still not fixed here.** More `__file__`-derived lookups remain, in inductor, in distributed, and in the testing helpers. All are `exists()`-guarded, so they degrade quietly rather than failing, and each wants its own decision. They are inventoried in #195887, together with the sites that were checked and deliberately excluded.

This PR was authored with the assistance of an AI coding assistant.

## Test Plan

**Linux, redirect-mode editable install (scikit-build-core 1.0.0), checkout holding a stale `_C`, 13 in-tree libraries and a `torch.egg-info`**, patch applied then reverted:

```
python test/test_utils.py -k TestTorchPathResolution -k test_cmake_prefix_path -v
```

5 passed against the pushed head. The warning listed all leftovers; `torch_parent` and `cmake_prefix_path` resolve to site-packages. scikit-build-core 1.0.0 has no `__loader__.paths`, so this exercises the `_C`-spec step end to end; the loader-paths step is pinned by `test_installed_torch_dir_prefers_the_editable_loader_paths` with a fake loader, including the case where the checkout appears in `paths` under a symlinked spelling.

**Windows, redirect-mode editable install (MSVC, Ninja, scikit-build-core 1.0.0), clean checkout**, run against the `_C`-spec revision:

```
python test\test_utils.py -k TestTorchPathResolution -k test_cmake_prefix_path -v
```

3 passed, 1 skipped (the global-deps test is a no-op on Windows); no warning; `cmake_prefix_path` resolves to site-packages with `TorchConfig.cmake` present.

**`cmake_prefix_path`** was also checked on a macOS arm64 editable install (scikit-build-core 1.0.3) by configuring a real project, since printing the path proves nothing when the stale value is a well-formed string:

```cmake
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.27)
project(probe LANGUAGES CXX)
find_package(Torch REQUIRED)
message(STATUS "PROBE_OK TORCH_LIBRARIES=${TORCH_LIBRARIES}")
```

configured with `-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=$(python -c 'import torch.utils; print(torch.utils.cmake_prefix_path)')`:

| tree | result |
| --- | --- |
| before | exit 1, "Could not find a package configuration file provided by Torch" |
| after | exit 0, `PROBE_OK`, `TORCH_LIBRARIES` resolved into site-packages |
| reverted | exit 1 again |

The inductor MPS path needs a Metal device and was not exercised; it is the same one-line change as the merged #195295. Building torch_openreg needs a full extension build and was not run; the change substitutes one directory computation for another, and both resolve to `<site-packages>/torch` in a wheel install.

Lint:

```
spin lint -- torch/_utils_internal.py torch/__init__.py torch/utils/__init__.py torch/_inductor/codegen/mps.py test/test_utils.py test/cpp_extensions/open_registration_extension/torch_openreg/setup.py
```

title: [Testcase Refactoring] Classify activation memory budget tests by hardware
body:
I reviewed the implementation and test results and confirm that the quoted description matches this change. Codex helped draft the quoted text.

> ### Summary
>
> Classify the activation memory budget tests by their hardware requirements, remove CUDA-specific device handling from the accelerator-generic cases, and preserve the optional Triton test behind a method-local runtime gate.
>
> Part of #185590.
>
> ### Changes
>
> - Split `MemoryBudgetTest` into `MemoryBudgetTest` (ACCELERATOR) and `MemoryBudgetBackendSpecificTest` (CUDA), with the corresponding `HardwareClassification` attributes.
> - Instantiate the accelerator-generic tests through the device-type test infrastructure, pass the generated device to tensor factories, and query allocator statistics through `torch.accelerator.memory_stats()`.
> - Keep `test_profile` in the CUDA class because its runtime estimator reaches `benchmark_gpu()`.
> - Keep `test_attention_vs_linear` in the CUDA class because its exact memory and FLOP assertions encode the CUDA SDPA cost model.
> - Keep `test_custom_triton_kernel` in the CUDA class because it defines a Triton kernel and explicitly creates CUDA tensors, and gate it with `@unittest.skipIf(not has_triton(), "test needs triton")`.
> - Remove the file-wide CUDA/Triton runner gate and keep the optional Triton requirement on its only consumer with `has_triton()`. Preserve the existing ROCm exclusion at the class level.
>
> ### Motivation
>
> Six tests exercise accelerator-independent activation memory budget behavior, but the original class selected CUDA globally. Using the device-type test infrastructure lets those tests run against supported accelerators while keeping CUDA-specific behavior in a narrowly scoped class. A method-local `has_triton()` gate prevents the optional Triton dependency from blocking unrelated tests.
>
> ### Test Plan
>
> Ran:
>
> ```bash
> .venv/bin/python -m py_compile test/functorch/test_ac.py
> .venv/bin/spin quicklint test/functorch/test_ac.py
> env PATH="$PWD/.venv/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin" SSL_CERT_FILE="$PWD/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/certifi/cacert.pem" .venv/bin/lintrunner -a test/functorch/test_ac.py
> git diff --check
> ```
>
> CI:
>
> ```bash
> python test/functorch/test_ac.py
> ```

title: [distributed] Skip TestDistBackend cases before spawning ranks
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.15.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #198157
* #198130
* __->__ #198366
* #198156
* #198158
* #198082
* #198066
* #198059
* #198049

`TestDistBackend` spawns rank workers before rank-side skip decorators run, so tests that always skip still pay for worker startup, temp directories and joins. Rank joins also sleep 100ms between status checks.

- `skip_if_small_worldsize`, `skip_if_no_gpu` and `skip_if_lt_x_gpu` mark their wrappers so `TestDistBackend.setUp` can skip in the parent when the same world-size condition holds or the build has no accelerator. Rank-side checks are unchanged.
- `MultiProcessTestCase` waits on process sentinels instead of sleeping; timeout and error handling are unchanged.
- `Barrier` polls every 10ms instead of 100ms.

Local runner time, identical outcomes:
- 66 NCCL/Gloo small-world-size cases: 129s -> 34s
- 155 CPU accelerator-only cases: 274s -> 23s
- 28 NCCL/Gloo lifecycle cases: 97s -> 90s

Test plan: CUDA build and lint; distributed_spawn CPU suite and NCCL/Gloo samples in normal and reverse order with identical pass/skip identities; five 8-rank Gloo cases still pass; sentinel normal-exit, early-error and watchdog paths.

title: CODEOWNERS: subscribe pearu to the linear_cross_entropy paths
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.13.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #195830
* __->__ #197876
* #196134
* #195829

The files dedicated to this op have no owner who works on them, so changes to
them reach pearu only by chance. Four narrower patterns subscribe pearu to the
seven files specific to the op.

> `/torch/_native/` covers the CuTeDSL package for slayton58 and drisspg,
> `/torch/nn/` covers the two nn.modules files for albanD and jbschlosser, and
> `/test/python_native/` is unowned. Each new pattern repeats the owners of the
> pattern it sits under rather than naming pearu alone: GitHub takes the last
> matching pattern and its owner list REPLACES the earlier one, so a bare
> `pearu` would have unsubscribed all four existing owners from those paths.
>
> Scope is the seven files dedicated to the op. It also has code in shared
> files, `torch/nn/functional.py` and `test/test_nn.py` among them, which
> path-based ownership cannot reach without subscribing to far more traffic
> than the op generates.
>
> The kernel module and its test arrive with #195829, so the patterns naming
> them match no committed path before that lands; this commit sits above it for
> that reason.

title: torch/_native: one CuTeDSL kernel for the chunked linear_cross_entropy backward
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.13.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #195830
* #197876
* #196134
* __->__ #195829

Per chunk the chunked path is three cuBLAS GEMM calls plus a set of pointwise
passes over the `(Bc, V)` logits buffer. This commit collects those passes into
one CuTeDSL kernel which also writes the dense gradient of logits into the
logits buffer itself, so the `index_add_` scatter and one buffer disappear.
Measured on an H100, the call takes 0.61-0.87 of eager's time at a lower peak
memory; on a B200, 0.30-0.78. The kernel is verified on sm_80, sm_90 and
sm_100, with its block knobs tuned on H100. Accuracy is level or better in
fp16; in bf16 the weight gradient's error runs 1.02x to 1.10x of eager's at the
same chunk size, from the same accumulation count.

> The `torch_nn::_linear_cross_entropy_batch_chunked` override stops delegating
> and computes the loss and gradients itself for the slice its `cond` claims.
> Per chunk: one cuBLAS matmul for the logits, one CuTeDSL kernel, and two more
> matmuls for the gradients.
>
> The kernel is what the change is about. Eager walks the `(Bc, V)` logits buffer
> five more times after the matmul -- row max, subtract, gather, `exp_`, row sum
> -- and then scatters the one-hot correction into `grad_linear_weight` with
> `index_add_`. Here one launch reads the raw logits twice (an online
> max-and-sumexp pass, then an apply pass) and writes the dense
> gradient-of-logits `g[n, v] = s_n * (softmax(z)[n, v] - [v == T_hat_n])`,
> emitting the two `(Bc,)` statistics the loss needs. Forming `g` densely is what
> makes both parameter gradients plain matmuls -- `grad_input = g @ W`,
> `grad_linear_weight = g^T @ X` -- so the scatter disappears: the backward is
> deterministic where eager's was not, and the separate `scatter_add` override
> stops being reachable from this path.
>
> `g` is written into the logits buffer's own storage rather than a second
> buffer, so a chunk costs one `(Bc, V)` buffer. That needs ordering, because
> `g[n, j]` occupies the bytes of `z[n, j / 2]`: pass 2 stages a group of column
> tiles in registers, synchronizes, and only then writes them, which is safe
> because a group's writes reach at most halfway into the columns it just read.
> The alternative that reaches the same footprint -- keeping the logits at low
> precision, as eager does for fp16 -- was measured and rejected for bf16: bf16
> stores `z` with absolute error ~|z| * 2^-9 while the softmax depends on
> DIFFERENCES of z, so gradients degrade once |z| reaches the tens, which is the
> regime a trained head operates in. At fp16 the buffer follows eager down to two
> bytes per element, since that is eager's own choice there and matching its
> footprint is the compatibility contract; the exponential and the scaled
> gradient still stay in fp32 registers, so this path is strictly more accurate
> than eager's at an identical footprint.
>
> Review `cutedsl_impl.py` first: it holds the eligibility predicate and the
> implementation, and it replaces the delegating implementation the routing commit
> installed. Eligibility is shapes, dtypes and device only, so it is safe under
> FakeTensor tracing; an input outside it never enters the override at all and the
> router falls back, which keeps "the kernel ran" observable rather than hidden
> behind an internal delegation. Its architecture condition is the DSL runtime's
> floor, which is also where this path's own arithmetic becomes available -- the
> logits matmul asks cuBLAS for an fp32 output from low-precision inputs, rejected
> below 8.0 -- and it lives in one predicate that `cond` and the tests both call.
> Holding out for a measurement on every capability would keep the kernel off
> hardware it runs on perfectly well; what is unmeasured below sm_90 is
> performance, not correctness.
>
> The implementation re-runs every check the op would have run -- an override
> installed at a backend key replaces the body that ran them, and the checks below
> it too -- by calling the op's own check functions, and it takes the per-row
> target correction and gradient weight the same way. Nothing about the op's
> contract is restated here; the previous commit moved each of those pieces out
> so this one could call them.
>
> Then `fused_grad_logits_kernel.py`: one block per row, because a row's own
> maximum and sum must be complete before any element of it can be written, and a
> block is the largest unit that can share them without a grid-wide barrier.
>
> Its two shape knobs -- the block width, and how many column tiles pass 2 stages
> per barrier -- are keyword arguments rather than constants, so a tuner or a
> caller with measured shapes can choose them without editing the file, and each
> combination compiles its own kernel. The defaults were measured on an H100 over
> a 3 x 5 grid at 20 chunk shapes, which the comment beside them summarizes: no
> setting wins everywhere, (512, 4) is never the worst and at most 1.39x behind
> the per-shape best, and since the chunked loop spends ~85% of its time in
> cuBLAS at the shapes where that share can be measured cleanly, the best setting
> at the loop's own chunk shapes is worth under 2% end to end. Their legal ranges
> are enforced, and one of them is a correctness limit rather than a preference
> -- above 32 warps per row the cross-warp combine would silently drop the
> surplus partials.
>
> Not covered here. The forward-only path (no gradient requested) has no `g` to
> write and keeps eager's statistics. `reduction='none'` keeps its own op and
> implementation. Probability targets, label smoothing, `acc_policy='accurate'`
> and fp32 input fall back through the router. One accuracy trade is worth
> naming: the dense `g` puts O(1) target-row contributions and O(1/V) off-target
> ones through a single matmul where eager keeps the scales apart, which costs
> ~14x on `grad_linear_weight` in isolation -- visible as ~15% at fp16 with
> `reduction='sum'`, invisible at bf16 where other error sources dominate. It
> buys the deleted scatter, the determinism and the speed.
>
> What the kernel buys, measured on an H100 through the op's own 12-shape sweep,
> in two comparisons.
>
> Against the op's own chunked path, at the same shapes and the same chunk size
> -- identical work, so this isolates the kernel: in bf16 the call takes
> 0.61-0.87 of eager's time (1.14-1.63x faster) at 0.77-0.97 of eager's peak
> memory; in fp16, 0.63-0.89 of the time at 0.86-1.00 of the peak.
>
> Accuracy splits by dtype. In fp16 the override is at least as accurate as
> eager everywhere: `grad_linear_weight` error is equal, 0.996-1.001 of
> eager's, and `grad_input` error is below it, 0.824-0.975. In bf16 the weight
> gradient is the one that gives ground -- 1.018-1.100 of eager's error,
> largest at `num_classes=16384` -- while `grad_input` stays level at
> 1.000-1.021. The dense `g^T @ X` accumulates in a different order than
> eager's `index_add_` scatter, which is where that comes from.
>
> The three matmuls are the same shapes at the same chunk size in both paths,
> so the whole win is in what surrounds them. Per chunk, eager makes five
> passes over the (Bc, V) logits buffer -- row max, subtract, exp, row sum, scale
> -- and then scatters the one-hot correction into grad_linear_weight with
> index_add_. Here one kernel reads the buffer twice and writes the dense
> gradient-of-logits once, and the dense form makes the scatter part of an
> ordinary matmul: less traffic and about a third of the launches (611 -> 195 per
> call at D=1024). The gain tracks how much of eager's time those passes were:
> 1.56x where the matmuls are cheap relative to the buffer (D=1024), 1.14x where
> they dominate (D=8192). Memory: one (Bc, V) fp32 buffer per chunk, with the
> gradient written into the same storage, replaces eager's logits buffer plus its
> downcast copy and its (Bc, D) scratch.
>
> Against liger-kernel 0.8.2, at constant memory: for each shape the override's
> chunk size is set so its peak matches liger's where that is reachable
> (0.997-1.025 of liger's peak at those points; elsewhere the whole batch fits
> one chunk and the peak stays at 0.48-0.87 of liger's). At that budget the
> override runs 1.25-6x faster than liger in bf16 (0.17-0.80 of its time) and
> 1.25-7x in fp16 (0.14-0.80), and 1.2-4x faster than eager at its default chunk
> size. The extra factor over the same-shape comparison is the memory itself: the
> override needs one (Bc, V) buffer per chunk where liger materializes more, so
> at equal peak it runs a chunk several times larger -- fewer chunks, fewer re-
> accumulations of grad_linear_weight, matmuls with a longer inner dimension. The
> chunk size stays under the caller's control; this comparison shows what the
> design returns when given liger's memory.
>
> This kernel's module imports the CuTeDSL runtime at import time, so the two
> tests that import every module under `torch/` --
> `test_public_bindings::test_modules_can_be_imported` and
> `test_testing::TestImports::test_circular_dependencies` -- need it in their
> optional-runtime ignore lists, where the other `_native` DSL kernels already
> sit. Both entries name the module rather than the package, so `cutedsl_impl`
> and the package `__init__` stay checked -- they import without the runtime
> and should keep having to.
>
> The new test files need the CuTeDSL runtime, so the B200 smoke job is the only
> place they can run at all -- nothing else collects them. That job already
> discovers every `test/python_native/test_*.py`, so they are picked up without
> being named. Added to it explicitly: `test_nn -k linear_cross_entropy`, the
> op's own accuracy harness. It compares fp16/bf16 against an fp64 reference
> with tolerances the op's author calibrated, and it runs in every CUDA job
> already -- but only where the DSL is installed does it measure this kernel
> instead of eager, so this job is where it earns its keep. The `-k` lines have
> to be named because `test_ops` and `test_nn` sit outside what that discovery
> reaches.
>
> Test Plan:
>
> The numbers above come from the out-of-tree benchmark harness, one process per
> configuration, over the same 12 shapes in both dtypes; the commands below are
> the in-tree correctness checks.
>
> ```
> python test/python_native/test_lce_fused_grad_logits_kernel.py
> python test/python_native/test_linear_cross_entropy_override.py
> python test/python_native/test_override_declarations.py
> python test/python_native/test_registry.py
> python test/test_nn.py -k linear_cross_entropy
> python test/test_ops.py -k linear_cross_entropy
> spin lint
> ```
>
> All of the above pass -- 54 kernel tests, 30 override tests -- including the
> two upstream batteries: `test_nn.py` runs 226 linear_cross_entropy tests and
> `test_ops.py` 191, both clean. Tests that
> need the kernel to be eligible skip where it is not, so a machine below its
> architecture floor reports skips rather than failures.
>
> The kernel's numerics are checked three ways. Against a torch expression of its
> contract, on its own, for three output dtypes across shapes that cross the block
> width and the staging group, including both aliasing ratios -- an fp32 buffer
> with narrower gradients, where a write lands halfway back, and the fp16 buffer
> where it lands on the column just read -- and including logits large enough
> that an unshifted exponential would overflow. End to end by the op's own
> fp64-referenced harness, which this change routes into the job that has the
> DSL. And two identical runs are required to produce bit-identical gradients,
> with `index_add_` asserted never to run, so the determinism the deleted scatter
> bought is pinned rather than asserted in prose.
>
> The op-level tests cover the paths a caller can reach rather than the kernel
> alone: the forward-only branch, which reimplements the loss with eager ops and
> which any `no_grad` call takes; `reduction='sum'`, a class weight and an
> `ignore_index` that fires, which are the four `_neg_weight_target` branches the
> row scale is built from; the empty batch, where the one allocation left
> unwritten has to be zeroed; and an out-of-range target, which traps as
> eager's index assert does, checked in a child process because the trap takes
> the CUDA context with it.

---
_🤖 Drafted by Claude Code (an AI agent) and reviewed & approved by pearu._

title: torch/_native: less per-call work in the chunked linear_cross_entropy loop
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.13.0) (oldest at bottom):
* #195830
* #197876
* __->__ #196134
* #195829

Three changes independent of the kernel's own arithmetic: `grad_linear_weight`
is no longer zeroed before the loop, because the first chunk writes it outright;
the kernel emits each row's loss contribution instead of the two statistics it
was built from, so the per-chunk loss arithmetic disappears; and the kernel's
staging default becomes `(512, 8)`. Together they are about 6% on top of the
kernel path on an H100 and about 10% on a B200, with every gradient bitwise
unchanged.

> None of the three changes what the loop computes. The first two remove work
> that existed only because of how the loop was written; the third changes only
> how the kernel schedules the work it already does.
>
> `grad_linear_weight` was allocated with `zeros` and then accumulated into,
> so the first chunk read back a (C, F) buffer that was known to be zero, after
> a (C, F) fill that nothing consumed. The first chunk now writes it with
> `mm(out=)` and later chunks accumulate as before, which drops a fixed
> `2 * C * F` bytes per call -- independent of the batch, the chunk size and the
> chunk count, so it reads as a share of call length: 4.8% at N=1024, 1.0% at
> N=16384. The accumulator is still zeroed when there is no first chunk to
> write it, which is the empty-batch early return.
>
> The kernel emitted `lse` and the target logit, and the caller then formed
> `scale * (lse - target_logit)` and reduced it, per chunk, on (Bc,) data:
> four launches moving 2 KB each. Both values are already in registers where
> the row's statistics are finished, so the kernel forms that product itself
> and writes one vector; the caller keeps one slot per row of the call and
> reduces once, after the loop, with `sum(out=loss)`. Nothing else read the two
> statistics, so they are gone from the kernel's signature. That slot is the one
> buffer here that is not a chunk, so the forward-only path -- which forms the
> loss chunk by chunk and never reads it -- does not allocate it.
>
> The staging default moves from `(512, 4)` to `(512, 8)` -- eight column tiles
> staged per barrier in pass 2 rather than four. `tiles_per_stage` does not
> reach pass 1's reduction, so this is a scheduling change and nothing else.
> Measured by calling the kernel directly from a captured CUDA graph, so that no
> GEMM time is in the number, over seven `(Bc, V)` chunk shapes -- `V` in
> {4096, 8192, 16384, 32000, 65536} at `Bc = 4096`, plus `Bc` in {1024, 2048} at
> `V = 32000` -- in both dtypes on an H100 and a B200, so 28 points: `(512, 8)`
> is faster at every one, by 1.4% to 12.2%, and uses less energy at every one,
> by 3.3% to 8.5%.
>
> Energy is worth reporting separately because it does not follow from the time.
> Per-call joules come from NVML's total-energy counter read over windows
> aligned to its updates, with the idle gaps subtracted at measured idle power.
> Where the board is not power-limited the faster setting draws 2-4% more power,
> so it saves less energy than time -- on B200 fp16, 9.1-12.2% faster for
> 6.9-8.5% less energy. Where the board is at its limit the two coincide: B200
> bf16 at `V >= 32000` runs both settings at ~1000 W, and there the energy win
> equals the time win. On H100 bf16 the faster setting also draws less power,
> 673 W against 691 W at `V=65536`, so it saves more energy (4.0%) than time
> (1.4%). Neither metric prefers `(512, 4)` at any point measured.
>
> That kernel is 4-25% of a chunked call and the rest is three cuBLAS GEMMs, so
> the retune is worth 0.1-2.9% end to end, largest where `in_features` is small
> relative to `num_classes`.
>
> Measured through the op's 12-shape sweep, paired per point across three
> repetitions -- the two states differ only in two Python files, so the arms are
> swapped in place at each point and a pair is measured seconds apart in one
> session.
>
> |                                    | H100 bf16 | H100 fp16 | B200 bf16 | B200 fp16 |
> | ---------------------------------- | --------- | --------- | --------- | --------- |
> | geomean                            | 1.058     | 1.065     | 1.095     | 1.099     |
> | min                                | 1.015     | 1.025     | 1.029     | 1.024     |
> | max                                | 1.143     | 1.160     | 1.377     | 1.390     |
> | above 1.0 in all three repetitions  | 11/12     | 12/12     | 12/12     | 12/12     |
>
> The maxima are at `in_features=1024` on the B200 and `V=4096` on the H100,
> where the fixed costs dominate; the minima are at `in_features=8192` and
> N=16384, where the surrounding GEMMs are largest. The single point not above
> 1.0 in every repetition is H100 bf16 at N=16384: 1.037 over a 0.992-1.042
> spread.
>
> Peak memory moves by at most the one new buffer, the (N,) fp32 loss terms:
> 0 to +48 kB measured, never more than `N * 4` bytes and sometimes nothing at
> all where the allocator reuses a freed block.
>
> The loss's summation order changes -- one reduction over N rather than a
> partial sum per chunk -- so the value is deterministic but not guaranteed
> bit-identical to a per-chunk accumulation. Measured against the previous path
> at four shapes spanning one to four chunks, in both dtypes, `grad_input`,
> `grad_linear_weight`, `grad_linear_bias` and the loss all came back bitwise
> identical.
>
> Test Plan:
>
> The kernel's isolation test asserts the loss term against a torch reference
> rather than against `lse` and the target logit separately. That pins the
> difference only: the row max cancels out of the term, and out of `g`, so what
> those assertions see of it is its effect on the row sum and not its value.
> Its other job, keeping `exp` in range, is pinned by
> `test_a_lone_high_column_pins_the_row_max`, where the row's maximum sits
> alone in one thread's column and a partial lost at either reduction stage
> takes the row out of fp32. The uniform-logit test became a stronger invariant
> in the process (`term == scale * log(V)`, whatever the logit value), and the
> aliased-buffer test still pins that the target logit is read before any write
> can occupy its bytes, since the term is now the only path by which that logit
> reaches an output.
>
> ```
> python test/python_native/test_lce_fused_grad_logits_kernel.py
> python test/python_native/test_linear_cross_entropy_override.py
> python test/test_nn.py -k linear_cross_entropy
> OPINFO_RESTRICT_TO_DSL=cutedsl python test/test_ops.py -k linear_cross_entropy
> lintrunner -m origin/main
> ```
>
> All pass on an H100 (sm_90) and a B200 (sm_100): 55 kernel tests, 31 override
> tests, 226 test_nn linear_cross_entropy tests, and the DSL-restricted test_ops
> run over its 5 OpInfo entries.

title: torch/_native: make an override's implementation selectable
body:
Stack from [ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack/tree/0.13.0) (oldest at bottom):
* __->__ #195830
* #197876
* #196134
* #195829

For benchmarking and testing we want to pin which implementation of an override
runs, including a passthrough that measures routing only. This commit adds that
selection mechanism to `torch._native`, and it is the last commit in the stack
so that it can be dropped without touching the kernel.

> An override registers one implementation per op. That is enough to ship a
> kernel, and not enough to measure one: the question "how much of this call is
> the kernel and how much is the dispatch that reaches it" cannot be answered
> while the only alternative to the kernel is not installing the override at all.
> Answering it needs a second implementation behind the same registration -- one
> that routes exactly as the kernel does and then delegates to the op -- and a way
> to pick between them per process or per block of code.
>
> `torch/_native/variants.py` is that selection: a store keyed on the qualified op
> name, a reserved name `"passthrough"`, a context manager, and
> `TORCH_NATIVE_OVERRIDE_VARIANTS` as an import-time initializer for the
> one-process-per-measurement protocol a benchmark harness needs. The env var is
> read once and malformed entries are dropped rather than raised on, because it
> must never be able to break `import torch`. `torch.backends.python_native`
> grows `set_override_variant` and `override_variant` beside the existing
> `disable_operations`, following the shape of `sdpa_kernel` and
> `preferred_linalg_library`.
>
> The linear_cross_entropy override then declares a table instead of a single
> implementation, and `cond` evaluates the SELECTED entry's eligibility. That
> detail is the point: an input the selected implementation cannot take never
> enters the override, so the router falls back and "the kernel ran" stays
> observable in a profile, rather than the override entering and delegating
> internally where no profile can see the difference.
>
> `passthrough` is NOT the fallback path -- ineligible inputs fall back through
> the router, as above, with no passthrough involved. It earns its place three
> other ways. It is the routing-cost baseline every performance comparison of
> this op needs, and the one that exposed a regression from an unrelated in-tree
> override. It is the live registration the next kernels land into: the
> no_reduction op is registered today with nothing but this implementation, so a
> kernel for it arrives as one more table entry with routing, harness and test
> plumbing already working. And it makes the routing test independent of the GPU
> it runs on, since pinning it removes the kernel's own architecture and dtype
> conditions from the question of whether the router installed the override.
>
> This is scaffolding with a horizon: as each task finds its best implementation
> the losers are deleted, and if the table ever holds one entry per op the
> machinery can go with it. It is a separate commit so that removal is a
> revert rather than an excavation.
>
> Test Plan:
>
> ```
> python test/python_native/test_variants.py
> python test/python_native/test_override_declarations.py
> python test/python_native/test_linear_cross_entropy_override.py
> python test/python_native/test_registry.py
> python test/test_nn.py -k linear_cross_entropy
> python test/test_ops.py -k linear_cross_entropy
> spin lint
> ```
>
> `test_variants.py` covers the store's behaviour without a GPU: default until
> selected, per-op independence, restoration after the context manager exits
> including after an exception, the backends surface, four malformed env-var
> forms, and the message an unknown name produces. The drift guard in
> `test_override_declarations.py` gains a check that the table covers exactly the
> registered ops and that every entry is callable -- DSL-free, so a typo cannot
> reach the hardware to be caught. The determinism test becomes parametrized over
> the implementations the table declares, discovered from it rather than listed,
> so a table edit needs no test edit; and the routing test is pinned to
> `passthrough` for the reason above.

title: Remove unload_xpu_triton_pyds() to fix fatal access violation in Windows+XPU inductor tests
body:
Windows+XPU inductor tests were crashing the test worker with an access violation (0xC0000005) during test teardown, inside fresh_cache()'s call to unload_xpu_triton_pyds(). See intel/torch-xpu-ops#4950.

The function manually dropped the last Python reference to the native spirv_utils "utils" object (`del driver_mod.driver.active.utils`) to force an immediate unload of spirv_utils.pyd. This could happen while native code from that same module was still on the call stack, unmapping the DLL out from under itself and causing the fatal access violation.

This manual unload is no longer needed: #159025 already added ignore_errors=is_windows() to the shutil.rmtree() call in fresh_cache(), so a still-mapped Triton .pyd no longer fails test cleanup. This PR removes unload_xpu_triton_pyds() and its call site entirely, letting the object be released normally by refcounting/GC.

title: [Testcase Refactoring] Make test_bisect_run_debuginfo device-agnostic via instantiate_device_type_tests
body:
## Summary

Make `test_bisect_run_debuginfo` in `test/dynamo/test_compiler_bisector.py` device-agnostic by migrating it into a new `TestCompilerBisectorDevice` instantiated via `instantiate_device_type_tests`.

Split from #191435 (refactoring this file for out-of-tree accelerator support).

## Changes

`test/dynamo/test_compiler_bisector.py`:
- New `TestCompilerBisectorDevice(TestCase)` (`hw_classification = HardwareClassification.ACCELERATOR`); `test_bisect_run_debuginfo` moves into it, and the hardcoded `device=GPU_TYPE` becomes the `device` argument injected by `instantiate_device_type_tests(TestCompilerBisectorDevice, globals(), except_for="cpu", allow_xpu=True)`.
- The Triton requirement stays gated by a device-blind `@unittest.skipIf(not has_triton(), "requires Triton")`; a fully device-aware gate needs a Triton `Capability` in the registry, left for a follow-up.
- The subprocess device is passed to the helper via `TORCH_BISECT_TEST_DEVICE` (the helper change shipped in the same #191435 split).

## Notes

This PR is self-contained: it includes the new-class scaffold (imports, `TestCompilerBisectorDevice`, the `instantiate_device_type_tests` call) so it is testable standalone. Unmigrated methods keep the old class guard and their non-`device` signatures, so instantiation leaves them untouched.
- MTIA coverage note: `HAS_GPU` could previously resolve to MTIA; no `MTIATestBase` exists for this file, so no MTIA variant is generated. Coverage note, not a regression on currently-tested devices.

## Motivation

The `@unittest.skipIf(not HAS_GPU)` class guard uses `HAS_GPU`, defined as `HAS_CUDA_AND_TRITON or HAS_XPU_AND_TRITON or HAS_MTIA_AND_TRITON`. Out-of-tree accelerators registered via `PrivateUse1` (e.g., Ascend NPU) are not in this list, so the whole test class gets skipped even though the tests only need a generic accelerator with Triton support. Using `instantiate_device_type_tests` with `except_for="cpu"` runs the tests on all non-CPU device types registered in the test framework, including out-of-tree backends, and `hw_classification` provides metadata for `--hw-classification` filtering.

## Test Plan

| Environment | Result |
|---|---|
| CPU-only (`torch-2.15-cpu`) | `pytest test/dynamo/test_compiler_bisector.py -q` -> **10 skipped**, collection identical to `main` |
| NPU (`torch-2.15-npu`, Ascend 910B4 / CANN 9.1.0 / triton-ascend 3.6.0), whole refactor applied | **11 passed, 0 failed** (3 generic + 8 `*_npu` device variants) |

title: [functorch] Decouple AOTDispatch tests from hardware-specific execution
body:
I reviewed the implementation and the AI-generated description below. It accurately describes the hardware-decoupling goal, the constrained class split, and the preservation of existing test coverage.

> ## Summary
>
> This PR hardware-decouples `test_aotdispatch.py` so that its generic and accelerator-wide AOTDispatch coverage can be reused by registered out-of-tree backends.
>
> It classifies the existing test classes as generic, CPU-specific, CUDA-specific, or accelerator-wide, and moves hardware-specific test methods into dedicated device-test templates. Eligible accelerator tests use an exclusion list instead of a device allowlist, allowing registered PrivateUse1 backends to participate without adding backend names to this file.
>
> ## Motivation
>
> The standard hardware-decoupling pattern is to split tests into hardware-homogeneous classes, add hardware-classification labels, instantiate device-generic classes, and rely on the capability-registration infrastructure for backend participation.
>
> `test_aotdispatch.py` cannot apply that pattern as a simple class split. Its main AOTAutograd suite is reused by Dynamo and cache variants through inheritance, and those variants also depend on `xfail_inherited_tests` and overridden execution helpers. In addition, device-test instantiation only materializes the test entries exposed by each template class. A direct split or ordinary inheritance-based decomposition would therefore risk changing test discovery, inherited expected-failure behavior, or which `run_autograd` and verification implementation executes.
>
> This change uses a constrained split:
>
> - The existing public generic classes and their shared helper methods remain in place.
> - Only tests with hardware-specific proof goals move into dedicated CUDA or accelerator classes.
> - Small private bases reuse the existing AOTAutograd, Dynamo, cache, partitioning, and module-simplified execution paths.
> - Explicit Dynamo and cache accelerator variants preserve the original overridden execution and inherited-xfail behavior.
> - Pure CPU classes remain CPU-specific and are not admitted to PrivateUse1.
>
> This keeps the existing mechanisms intact while separating hardware policy from the generic test suites.
>
> Capability registration is not needed here. The refactor is constrained by test discovery, inherited xfail behavior, and Dynamo/cache helper selection, none of which capability gates control. After splitting, device eligibility is fully determined by the device matrix and existing skips; there are no optional runtime capability consumers.
>
> ## Changes
>
> - Add `HardwareClassification` metadata to the existing generic and CPU-specific test classes.
> - Split CUDA-only AOTAutograd, partitioning, and module-simplified tests into CUDA-classified classes.
> - Split CPU-plus-accelerator tests into accelerator-classified device-test templates.
> - Preserve the existing Dynamo and cache execution paths for the split AOTAutograd tests.
> - Replace accelerator allowlisting with backend exclusions, currently retaining the existing HPU exclusion.
> - Add the PrivateUse1 autocast dispatch registration needed by the accelerator-wide autocast tests.
>
> Existing test coverage and test behavior for CPU, CUDA/ROCm, MPS, XPU, HPU, and the other previously covered devices are unchanged. No existing test is removed from its applicable hardware scope. The only coverage expansion is admission of eligible registered PrivateUse1 backends.
>
> #198365 extracts the class split and hw_classification labels from this PR as a separate structural change. After #198365 lands, rebase this PR on it so the device parameterization and Triton admission changes can be reviewed here on their own.
>
> ## Test Plan
>
> Ran:
>
> ```bash
> PATH="$PWD/.venv/bin:$PATH" .venv/bin/lintrunner -a test/functorch/test_aotdispatch.py
> python3 -m py_compile test/functorch/test_aotdispatch.py
> git diff --check
> ```
>
> CI:

> ## Summary
>
> This PR decouples Triton tests from a process-wide GPU selection so
> accelerator-common coverage can run on eligible registered backends, including
> PrivateUse1, while preserving CUDA- and XPU-specific semantics.
>
> ## Design
>
> - Mixed proof targets are separated with `HardwareClassification`: GENERIC for
>   device-independent analysis, ACCELERATOR for portable accelerator behavior,
>   and exact CUDA/XPU classifications for backend-specific semantics.

>   CUDA-only query.
> - Device-independent mutation analysis remains GENERIC, while the custom TMA
>   launcher keeps separate accelerator and Triton-CPU-fallback coverage.
> - Large specialized test blocks remain at their original locations, with
>   additional class boundaries and a helper-only `_KernelTestsBase`. This keeps
>   the PR below the 2,000-line sanity limit without changing assertions,
>   parameterization, or device matrices.

title: [Feature Refactoring][dynamo] Add capability-gate tests and hw_classification labels for test_streams.py
body:
## Summary

#197187 made the cross-stream `sync_dealloc` emission in
`InstructionTranslatorBase._maybe_emit_sync_dealloc`
(torch/_dynamo/symbolic_convert.py) capability-based: the device whitelist
`("cuda", "mtia", "xpu")` became a current-accelerator check, so out-of-tree
multi-stream accelerators (e.g. NPU) get the `streams::record_event` +
`streams::sync_dealloc` emission on cross-stream `del`. That PR landed the
production change without tests, and `test/dynamo/test_streams.py` carries no
`hw_classification` labels.

This PR adds both, with no production-code changes:

- 4 CPU-only gate-contract tests in a new `TestStreamsSyncDeallocDeviceGate`
  (GENERIC): cpu `del` never emits — regression anchor; meta `del` skips
  gracefully through the current-accelerator check; a stream-capable device
  outside the old whitelist emits, with exact op arguments asserted;
  `get_current_stream` failures on a supported device propagate — pinning the
  no-exception-probing design of #197187.
- `hw_classification` labels for all 5 test classes in the file
  (GENERIC / ACCELERATOR / CUDA / XPU), following #190991.

## Changes

- `test/dynamo/test_streams.py` (+157): the 4 gate-contract tests above
  (hardware-classification GENERIC; direct calls into the production
  `_maybe_emit_sync_dealloc` with a real `torch.fx.Graph`, and end-to-end
  `extract_graph` runs for the cpu/meta anchors) + labels for all 5 test
  classes in the file.

## Not changed

- No production code is touched — the gate itself is #197187's
  (current-accelerator check, no exception-based probing).

## Test plan

      probe emits `streams::record_event` + `streams::sync_dealloc` under the

      re-validated on the capability gate).

title: [CPU] Add RVV vectorized kernel for FusedAdam (float/double)
body:
## Motivation

CPU FusedAdam expresses its math through `at::vec::Vectorized`, which has no RVV backend: on riscv64 the generic `Vectorized<T>` degrades to element-wise scalar loops, and the `blendv`-based lerp in `adam_math` blocks even compiler autovectorization. This patch adds a kernel-local RVV implementation following the pattern of the previously merged DepthwiseConvKernel RVV kernel ([PR #127867](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/127867)). Because the new code is guarded by `__riscv_v_intrinsic >= 12000`, default riscv64 builds (rv64gc, no V) and all other platforms compile it out with zero impact — upstream CI stays green.

## Build & Test Environment

```bash
# build
export USE_CUDA=0
export USE_DISTRIBUTED=0
export USE_MKLDNN=0
export MAX_JOBS=32
export CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang++
export CMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang
export CMAKE_C_FLAGS=-march=rv64gcv
export CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS=-march=rv64gcv
pip3 install --upgrade typing_extensions scikit-build-core
pip3 install --no-build-isolation -v -e .

# full-fused sweep (all 94 cases)
python3 -m pytest test/test_optim.py -k "fused" -q
```

Toolchains actually used: clang-21.1.7 & Python-3.11

> ## Summary
>
> Move existing Triton heuristic tests into classes by proof goal and add hardware classification labels. This is the structural portion of #193340.
>
> ## Scope
>
> - Separate generic tests, accelerator runtime and backend configuration tests, and ROCm-specific tests.
> - Separate cached-autotuning loading tests from runtime cache interaction tests.
> - Preserve existing test bodies, device selection, and skip gates. The one moved test that used a fixture through `self` now references the fixture on its original class.

> #193340 will follow this PR and can then focus on device injection and Triton admission without repeating these class moves.
